To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Fast Greedy Equivalence Search algorithm is an efficient and scalable method for learning the gene regulatory network of the human brain from expression data, and that the method is available publicly at NeuroSuites.
the merging of locally learned gene regulatory networks is a fast and scalable way to learn the structure of genome wide networks.

we present a new approach to learning the structure of genome-wide gene regulatory networks, based on merging of locally learned subnetworks, which outperforms state of the art algorithms in both recall and speed.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of learning a genome-wide gene regulatory network for the brain.
learning interpretable genome wide regulatory networks from large datasets.
developing new methods for learning gene networks from high dimensional data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

we have developed a new algorithm for learning the structure and parameters of gene regulatory networks, which is competitive with state of the art algorithms in terms of recall of the true network structure and is also much faster and scalable to large numbers of variables.
the proposed method for learning a genome wide gene regulatory network from the Allen Human Atlas is a significant contribution in terms of scalability, speed, interpretability and recall.
we have developed an efficient method to learn gene regulatory networks from data that scales to the genome wide level and is competitive with state of the art methods in recall.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we developed new tools to learn interpretable genome wide models from large scale biological experiments and that we applied these to a large scale experiment to learn a genome wide regulatory model for the human brain.

we developed a new method for structure learning in Bayesian networks, we solved a problem of inference in Bayesian networks and we applied this to the problem of learning gene regulatory networks in the human brain.
we developed a new algorithm for learning gene regulatory network that is competitive and scalable.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Bayesian networks can be used to learn interpretable gene regulatory networks for large numbers of genes and they can also be used for inference in these large models.
the merging approach is very promising in learning gene regulatory networks and can be applied to other domains as well.
the merging of Bayesian networks can be used for learning genome wide regulatory networks, while also providing a scalable tool for Bayesian inference.
